nameStory: This woodsorrel earned its 'great' and 'large' names by being one of the biggest members of its family in eastern North America. The 'woodsorrel' part comes from the sour, lemony taste of its leaves - 'sorrel' means sour in Old French, and this plant loves growing in wooded areas.
description: Great yellow woodsorrel is an annual herb that stands out as one of the larger woodsorrels you might encounter in New England's forests. Like its smaller cousins, it has the classic three-leaflet clover-like leaves and cheerful yellow flowers that bloom in late spring. This plant grows low to the ground but spreads wider than most other woodsorrels, forming patches in the understory of sandy woodlands.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals bloom from May to June, each flower about the size of a dime with delicate reddish veins running through the petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets arranged like a shamrock, each leaflet noticeably larger than other woodsorrels and soft to the touch with a distinctly sour, lemony taste when chewed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads wider and grows more robust than other woodsorrels, forming loose patches rather than tight clumps

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, pointed seed capsules that explosively pop open when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away when touched

habitat: Great yellow woodsorrel prefers sandy soils in open woodlands and forest edges, particularly in areas with good drainage. In New England, look for it in mixed hardwood forests with sandy or alluvial soils, often near streams or in areas where the forest floor gets dappled sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in early spring as the weather warms, followed by the distinctive yellow flowers from May into June.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the characteristic explosive seed pods develop and mature, while the leafy growth continues through the summer months.
seasonality.fall: As an annual plant, great yellow woodsorrel begins to die back in fall after releasing its seeds.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, as this annual completes its life cycle and overwinters only as seeds in the soil.

funFact: Great yellow woodsorrel's seed pods are like tiny botanical cannons - when ripe, they can shoot their seeds up to 10 feet away with enough force that you can actually hear the 'pop' when they explode, earning woodsorrels the nickname 'touch-me-nots' among some nature enthusiasts.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other yellow-flowered woodsorrels, but great yellow woodsorrel's notably larger leaves and more robust growth habit help distinguish it. Remember: 'great' means greater size in both leaves and overall plant spread compared to its cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'great' yellow woodsorrel, this species is actually quite rare in New England with only a couple documented observations, making it more of a botanical treasure hunt than a common find for most nature explorers.
compareHints: Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit. While mountain woodsorrel has white or pink flowers and upright yellow woodsorrel tends to grow more vertically, great yellow woodsorrel spreads wider with distinctly larger, more robust foliage than any of its New England cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
